title: The Debate and the Two Garlands
word: each as a lens for a week
hook: Shankara comes to debate Mandana Mishra, and Mandana's wife holds the garlands: the last pair, Mimamsa and Vedanta, and a verse Hindus say before meals
carry: brahmarpanam: every act, even a meal, offered to brahman
tomorrow: a scholar forgets his wife, then names a book for her.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line, samkhya and yoga: the seer is not the storm. Kapila taught it to his mother. Today, the last pair.
screen: `THE SEER IS NOT THE STORM.` · `THE LAST PAIR.`

segments.voice: This one comes from a later life of Shankara, so hold it as legend. The young teacher of Vedanta walks into the town of Mahishmati, looking for the greatest scholar of Mimamsa, Mandana Mishra. How will he find the house? Look for the one, people tell him, where even the parrots at the door argue about whether the Veda stands on its own authority. The two men debate for days. The judge is Mandana's own wife, Ubhaya Bharati, a scholar herself. She puts a fresh garland around each man's neck. Whoever's garland wilts first, she says, has lost. Ritual against knowledge: the last pair of lenses.
screen: `LOOKING FOR MANDANA MISHRA.` → `PARROTS AT THE DOOR.` → `THE JUDGE AND TWO GARLANDS.`

segments.voice: Mandana's school is Mimamsa. Its question: what is this act for? Mimamsa reads the Veda as a book of things to do: rites done rightly, in order, many of them daily. Shankara's school is Vedanta. Its question: what does all of it rest on? For Shankara, rites purify the heart, but freedom comes from knowing Brahman, the one reality under everything. In the legend, Mandana's garland fades first, and he becomes Shankara's student. But Mimamsa didn't vanish. Hindu homes still keep daily rites, and priests still ask how a rite is done rightly. And one verse holds both lenses. Many Hindu families say it before they eat. It's from the Bhagavad Gita, chapter four. In paraphrase: the offering is Brahman. The food offered is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire that is Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in every act reaches Brahman. Mimamsa recognizes every piece: an offering, a fire, the one who offers. Vedanta sees what each piece rests on. That's the teaching under today. In Hinduism, an ordinary act, even eating, can be an offering. Many teachers read the verse at the table this way: the plate is the offering, the hunger is the fire, and the eater is the one who offers. None of it is outside Brahman. Some families say it aloud; some just fold their hands. Either way, dinner stops being just fuel.
screen: `WHAT IT'S FOR, WHAT IT RESTS ON.` · `ONE VERSE HOLDS BOTH LENSES.` · `THE OFFERING IS BRAHMAN.` · `A MEAL CAN BE AN OFFERING.`

segments.voice: Before your next meal, or right now with a glass of water, pause before the first bite or sip. Families who say the verse begin with one word, brahmarpanam, the offering is Brahman. You can say that word, or simply look at the food, the hand and the hunger, and see them as one offering. If you pray, offer the meal to the One you pray to; if you don't, take the first bite in full thanks.
Each as a lens for a week. Today, the third pair: Mimamsa asks what this act is for, Vedanta asks what it all rests on. Today's word.
screen: `EACH AS A LENS FOR A WEEK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: brahmarpanam, every act, even a meal, offered to Brahman. The garlands faded; the verse is still said at the table. That's today, done.
